title: 17 CFR Ch. II (4-1-25 Edition), Part 275, § 275.202(a)(11)(G)-1, Family offices
publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office; rule issued by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
publication_date_or_edition: 2025 annual CFR edition, revised April 1, 2025; 17 CFR § 275.202(a)(11)(G)-1. The original adopting release is SEC IA-3220, 76 FR 37983 (2011).
jurisdictions: United States federal; Investment Advisers Act of 1940
entity_roles: Family office and persons receiving investment advice from it
accounting_bases: Investment-adviser regulatory perimeter; not an accounting standard
source_classification: Binding federal regulation in official annual codification
inspected_summary: The rule limits the exclusion to a family office as defined in the section, for purposes of the Act. Paragraph (b) requires no clients other than family clients, family-client ownership and family-member/family-entity control, and no public holding-out as an investment adviser. It includes a one-year transition provision for a non-family client resulting from death or an involuntary transfer. These conditions do not establish that any actual office qualifies or answer state or other regulatory questions.

title: Why the family office of the future needs refreshed operating models
publisher: Ernst & Young LLP (EY US); Catherine Fankhauser and Paul McKibbin, EY family-office advisers
publication_date_or_edition: Published September 30, 2024; article reflects EY US views on the Wharton Global Family Alliance 2024 Family Office Benchmarking Report

accounting_bases: Family-office operations, governance, cyber risk, succession, and external-provider coordination; no accounting standard
source_classification: Practitioner-authored secondary interpretation of a named survey plus recommendations; not the full survey report or independent assurance
inspected_summary: The article recommends parallel family and office governance with clear communication. Its survey summary reports that about 40% of respondents had a formal office-leadership succession plan and about 20% had formal plans for the family and professional office management; it also reports that about one quarter said family-office or personnel data had been compromised and that 75% had experienced phishing. These are respondent-reported signals, not population estimates or evidence that controls failed in a particular office.

title: Three Lines Model: Assurance and Advice in Support of Effective Governance
publisher: The Institute of Internal Auditors (The IIA), Global Board of Directors
publication_date_or_edition: Statement of Position published July 8, 2026; replaces the former Three Lines Model position paper
jurisdictions: General organizational governance; professional model, not jurisdiction-specific law
entity_roles: Governing body, senior management, specialist/support functions, internal audit, and external assurance providers
accounting_bases: Governance, risk management, compliance, controls, assurance, and advisory roles
source_classification: Current professional association Statement of Position; not a legal or accounting mandate
inspected_summary: Management owns day-to-day risk and designs and operates processes and controls. Specialist second-line roles support, monitor, and challenge. Internal audit provides independent assurance without taking management responsibility. The model should fit organizational size, complexity, risks, and obligations. Outsourcing may supply skills or capacity, but it does not change the governing body's accountability for effective direction and oversight. The IIA says internal audit is not required for every organization.

title: NIST SP 1300, NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Small Business Quick-Start Guide
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S. Department of Commerce
publication_date_or_edition: SP 1300 final, published February 26, 2024; supplement to NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
jurisdictions: U.S. federal publication; guidance also designed for small and medium businesses and other relatively small organizations
entity_roles: Small-organization leadership, staff, IT administrators, and service providers
accounting_bases: Cybersecurity risk management, information assets, incident response, and recovery; not accounting standards
source_classification: Official NIST voluntary quick-start guidance; not regulation, certification, or family-office-specific evidence
inspected_summary: The guide's IT inventory asks for system/service owner or administrator, use, sensitive data, MFA status, and impact if access is lost. It recommends restricting access, MFA for sensitive accounts such as banking, accounting/tax, email, and password managers, patching, encryption, backups and restore tests, and monitoring. Its incident and recovery sections call for named authority and contacts, communications, internal/external recovery roles, prioritization, backup-integrity checks, after-action review, and a recovery playbook covering people, facilities, technical systems, and external services.
